themeName: Theme 3: Business Behaviour and the Labour Market

topics.title: Normal Profits, Supernormal Profits and Losses

cards.front: Why do firms grow — and why do some stay small?
cards.back:
The underlying incentive is profit. Growth brings economies of scale, market power over prices and suppliers, easier access to finance, and stronger brand recognition.

Firms stay small because of diseconomies of scale, market conditions (niche or fiercely competitive markets), or owner preference — keeping control and a manageable lifestyle over expansion.

cards.front: Explain the principal-agent problem and the divorce of ownership and control.
cards.back:
In large firms the owners (shareholders) do not run the business — managers do.

This separation of ownership and control means managers may pursue their own objectives — higher salaries, sales maximisation, perks — instead of the owners' goal of profit maximisation.

Solutions align incentives: performance-related pay, bonuses and stock options that make managers gain when shareholders do.

cards.front: Distinguish public from private sector, and profit from not-for-profit organisations.
cards.back:
• Public sector — owned and funded by the government, usually to provide services in the public interest (the NHS).
  • Private sector — owned by individuals or shareholders, usually profit-motivated.

Profit organisations aim to generate financial returns for owners.

Not-for-profit organisations, such as charities, reinvest any surplus in their social purpose instead.

cards.front: Distinguish organic from inorganic growth.
cards.back:
Organic growth is growth generated from within the business using its own resources — new products, new locations, more market share. Slower, but controlled.

Inorganic growth is growth achieved through mergers or takeovers of other businesses — faster, but riskier: integration can fail, cultures can clash, and the price paid may exceed the value gained.

cards.front: Distinguish horizontal, vertical and conglomerate integration.
cards.back:
• Horizontal — merging with a competitor at the same stage of production (two car manufacturers), raising market share.
  • Vertical — merging along the supply chain: backward with a supplier (a car maker buying a tyre maker) to secure inputs; forward with a distributor to secure outlets and margin.
  • Conglomerate — merging with an unrelated business, spreading risk across markets.

cards.front: What constrains business growth?
cards.back:
• Market size — niche or saturated markets cap expansion, pushing firms to internationalise.
  • Access to finance — smaller firms look riskier, so borrowing is harder and dearer.
  • Owner objectives — lifestyle goals or satisficing over rapid growth.
  • Regulation — competition policy (the CMA) can block mergers that create too much market power, and rules on demerit goods can cap whole markets.

cards.front: What is a demerger, and why do firms demerge?
cards.back:
A demerger is when a large firm splits into two or more separate, independent businesses — the opposite of a merger.

Reasons:

  • Reduce diseconomies of scale.
  • Increase focus on the core business.
  • Resolve culture clashes from an earlier merger.
  • Shed loss-making divisions.
  • Raise capital.
  • Regulatory pressure — the CMA can force a demerger to cut monopoly power.

cards.front: Evaluate the impacts of a demerger on the business, workers and consumers.
cards.back:
• Business — lower average costs and sharper focus, against transition costs and lost synergies.
  • Workers — better conditions and career paths in focused firms, against redundancies and transition uncertainty.
  • Consumers — more competition can mean lower prices and better service; but smaller firms may lose scale economies, which can push costs and prices the other way.

cards.front: Name the four business objectives, with their rules.
cards.back:
• Profit maximisation — the traditional assumption, maximising shareholder returns: produce where MC = MR.
  • Revenue maximisation — for market share or scale economies: MR = 0.
  • Sales maximisation — grow volume while breaking even: AC = AR.
  • Satisficing — a satisfactory rather than maximum profit, balancing shareholders against managers' own objectives (the principal-agent problem); output and price lie between the profit-max and sales-max positions.

cards.front: Show profit maximisation on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
Profit is maximised at the output Q where MC = MR: below Q each extra unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond Q it adds more cost than revenue.

Read the price P off the AR curve at Q and average cost C off the AC curve — with P above C, the gap times Q is supernormal profit.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the profit-maximising point marked where MC crosses MR at output Q, price P read from AR and average cost C from AC

cards.front: Show revenue maximisation on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
Total revenue is maximised at the output where MR = 0 — the point where MR crosses the quantity axis. Up to Q every unit still adds revenue; beyond it, MR is negative and revenue falls.

Firms may choose this to build market share or reach scale economies — output is higher and price lower than at profit max, and profit is sacrificed while revenue peaks.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the revenue-maximising point marked where MR crosses the quantity axis at output Q, price P read from AR

cards.front: Show sales maximisation on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
The largest output a firm can sell without making a loss is where AC = AR: price just equals average cost, so the firm breaks even and earns only normal profit.

Motives: market share, clearing stock, or limit pricing — a price too low for potential entrants to match profitably. Output is the highest of the three objectives, price the lowest.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the sales-maximising point marked where AC crosses AR at output Q, with price equal to average cost

cards.front: Why might a firm satisfice rather than maximise profit?
cards.back:
Because of the principal-agent problem: managers may prefer higher salaries, job security or perks, and choose a profit level acceptable to shareholders while meeting their own goals. In small firms, owners may satisfice to protect work-life balance.

On the diagram, a satisficing firm's output and price sit between the profit-maximising and sales-maximising positions — enough profit to satisfy, not the maximum available.

cards.front: Define and give the formulas for total, average and marginal revenue.
cards.back:
• TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings from sales.
  • AR = TR ÷ Q — which simplifies to the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve.
  • MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the additional revenue from selling one more unit.
cards.formulaHtml: TR=P×Q;AR=TR/Q;MR=ΔTR/ΔQTR = P × Q; AR = TR/Q; MR = ΔTR/ΔQTR=P×Q;AR=TR/Q;MR=ΔTR/ΔQ

cards.front: Show the revenue curves in perfect competition.
cards.back:
Firms are price takers, selling every unit at the market price, so demand is perfectly elastic: D = AR = MR = P, one horizontal line.

With price fixed, total revenue rises at a constant rate — a straight ray from the origin.
cards.svgAlt: Horizontal line at price P labelled D=AR=MR=P, with a straight total revenue ray rising from the origin

cards.front: Show the revenue curves in imperfect competition.
cards.back:
Firms are price makers but must cut price to sell more, so AR (the demand curve) slopes down and MR lies below AR — in a linear diagram, twice as steep.

TR therefore rises at a decreasing rate, peaks exactly where MR = 0 (quantity Q), and falls beyond it as MR turns negative.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping AR with a steeper MR crossing the quantity axis at Q, and a total revenue curve peaking directly above Q

cards.front: State the total revenue rule linking PED to pricing decisions.
cards.back:
If demand is price elastic (PED > 1), cutting price raises TR and raising price lowers it. If demand is price inelastic (PED < 1), raising price raises TR. At unitary elasticity (PED = 1), price changes leave TR unchanged.

On the imperfect-competition diagram: demand is elastic above the TR peak, inelastic beyond it — MR = 0 marks the boundary.

cards.front: Define the seven cost measures.
cards.back:
• Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries).
  • Variable costs vary directly with it (raw materials, hourly wages).
  • TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output:

  • AC = TC ÷ Q.
  • AFC = TFC ÷ Q.
  • AVC = TVC ÷ Q.

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the additional cost of producing one more unit.
cards.formulaHtml: TC=TFC+TVC;AC=TC/Q;MC=ΔTC/ΔQTC = TFC + TVC; AC = TC/Q; MC = ΔTC/ΔQTC=TFC+TVC;AC=TC/Q;MC=ΔTC/ΔQ

cards.front: A firm has fixed costs of £200. Variable costs are £80 at 10 units, £140 at 20, £250 at 30 and £400 at 40. Calculate TC and AC at each output, and MC between each step.
cards.back:
TC = 200 + TVC: 280, 340, 450, 600

AC = TC ÷ Q:

  • 280 ÷ 10 = £28
  • 340 ÷ 20 = £17
  • 450 ÷ 30 = £15
  • 600 ÷ 40 = £15

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ:

  • (340 − 280) ÷ 10 = £6
  • then £11
  • then £15

Note where AC stops falling: between 30 and 40 units MC equals AC at £15 — average cost bottoms out exactly where marginal cost catches it.

cards.front: Draw the short-run cost curves, and explain their shapes.
cards.back:
Diminishing marginal productivity shapes them all: with at least one factor fixed, extra workers eventually add less and less output, so MC falls briefly then rises — and the average curves are U-shaped.

MC cuts both AVC and AC at their minimum points: while MC is below an average it drags it down, once above it pulls it up. AFC falls continuously as fixed costs spread over more units.
cards.svgAlt: J-shaped MC curve cutting the AVC and AC curves at their minimum points, with AFC falling continuously

cards.front: Show the relationship between short-run and long-run average cost curves.
cards.back:
Each SRAC curve represents one scale of plant — fixed in the short run. In the long run all factors are variable, so the firm can choose any plant size: the LRAC is the envelope of the SRAC curves, touching each from below.

Moving down the LRAC means growing onto bigger, cheaper plants (economies of scale); beyond the minimum, further scale raises average costs.
cards.svgAlt: U-shaped LRAC curve as the envelope of three short-run average cost curves, with SRAC2 touching at the LRAC minimum

cards.front: Name the six types of internal economies of scale.
cards.back:
• Purchasing — bulk-buying discounts.
  • Technical — large-scale machinery affordable only at volume.
  • Managerial — specialist managers.
  • Financial — cheaper borrowing as lenders see less risk.
  • Marketing — advertising spread over more units.
  • Risk-bearing — diversification across products and markets.

All are reasons within the business why average costs fall as output grows — they drive the LRAC's falling section.

cards.front: Show economies and diseconomies of scale on the LRAC curve, and mark the MES.
cards.back:
The falling section is economies of scale; the rising section is diseconomies, where size breeds bureaucracy, communication failures and weaker coordination.

The minimum efficient scale is the lowest output at which the lowest possible long-run average cost is reached — the bottom of the curve. Its position matters for market structure: a high MES leaves room for only a few efficient firms.
cards.svgAlt: U-shaped LRAC curve with the economies-of-scale section falling, diseconomies rising, and the minimum efficient scale marked at the bottom

cards.front: Distinguish internal from external economies of scale.
cards.back:
Internal economies arise within the business — its own scale lowers its own average costs (purchasing power, technical scale, and the rest).

External economies arise outside the business: the whole industry's growth lowers costs for every firm in it — a skilled local labour pool, specialist suppliers clustering nearby, shared infrastructure. Internal economies move a firm along its LRAC; external economies shift the whole curve down.

cards.front: Why do diseconomies of scale set in?
cards.back:
Size itself becomes the cost driver:

  • Communication stretches across more layers and sites.
  • Coordination and control weaken as management grows remote from operations.
  • Motivation falls when workers feel like small parts of a vast machine.
  • Bureaucracy multiplies.

This is why growth is not automatically profitable — and why some firms demerge to get back below the point where average costs turn upward.

cards.front: Define normal profit, supernormal profit and loss.
cards.back:
Normal profit is the minimum profit required to keep a firm in the industry: TR = TC, the break-even point.

Supernormal profit is any profit above normal profit, so TR > TC. A loss is when TR < TC.

cards.front: Why is normal profit counted as a cost — and where does a firm earning only normal profit sit on a diagram?
cards.back:
Normal profit is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur staying in this industry, so it is already counted inside the firm's costs rather than added on top.

On a diagram the firm sits where AR = AC: breaking even in economic terms, even though its accounts would show a positive profit figure. Only the area above AC is supernormal profit.

cards.front: Show supernormal profit on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
The firm produces at Q where MC = MR, charges the price P read off AR, and has average cost C read off AC at that output.

With P above C, the shaded rectangle (P − C) × Q is supernormal profit — profit beyond the normal profit already counted inside costs.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with output at MC equals MR, the price from AR above average cost from AC, and the rectangle between them up to output Q shaded as supernormal profit

cards.front: Show a loss on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
The firm still produces where MC = MR — now the loss-minimising output. The price P comes off AR and average cost C off AC, but here C sits above P.

The shaded rectangle (C − P) × Q is the loss. Whether the firm keeps producing depends on the shut-down rules.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram where average cost from AC sits above the price from AR at the loss-minimising output, with the rectangle between them up to Q shaded as the loss

cards.front: State the short-run and long-run shut-down rules.
cards.back:
Short run — fixed costs must be paid even at zero output, so compare price with average variable cost. If AR > AVC, keep producing: revenue covers all variable costs and contributes towards fixed costs. If AR < AVC, shut down immediately — the loss would exceed total fixed costs.

Long run — all costs are variable, so compare price with average cost: if AR < AC, exit the industry.

cards.front: Show the short-run shut-down condition on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
At the output where MC = MR, the price read off AR lies below AVC: revenue does not even cover variable costs, so producing makes the loss worse than paying fixed costs alone, and the firm shuts down immediately.

With P between AVC and ATC it would keep operating in the short run, covering its variable costs and contributing towards fixed costs; in the long run it needs P to reach AC or it exits.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with ATC and AVC curves both above the demand curve, so at the output where MC equals MR the price is below average variable cost and the firm shuts down in the short run

cards.front: Define allocative efficiency and productive efficiency.
cards.back:
Allocative efficiency: production where AR = MC (D = S) — resources go to the optimal mix of goods and services for society's wants and needs, maximising society's welfare.

Productive efficiency: production at the lowest point on the average cost curve, where MC = AC — costs of production are minimised.

cards.front: Define dynamic efficiency and X-inefficiency.
cards.back:
Dynamic efficiency requires supernormal profits in the long run: firms reinvest them in research and development, improving product quality and productive efficiency over time.

X-inefficiency comes from a lack of competition or profit incentive: the firm grows organisationally slack, so its average costs sit higher than they need to be.

cards.front: Define static efficiency.
cards.back:
Static efficiency: resources are both allocated and utilised in the most efficient way possible at a given point in time.

It requires both allocative and productive efficiency — the two conditions that can hold at a single moment, unlike dynamic efficiency, which is about improvement over time.

cards.front: Show efficiency in perfect competition in long-run equilibrium.
cards.back:
The horizontal price line is tangent to the minimum of AC, and MC passes through the same point:

  • P = MC gives allocative efficiency.
  • Minimum AC gives productive efficiency.

Both sit at the same output Q.

But with only normal profit there is nothing to reinvest, so dynamic efficiency is unlikely.
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition long-run diagram with the horizontal price line tangent to the minimum of the average cost curve where marginal cost also crosses, marking the productively and allocatively efficient points at the same output

cards.front: Show why a firm with market power is allocatively and productively inefficient.
cards.back:
Profit-maximising at MC = MR, the firm stops short of both efficient points:

  • P > MC, so there is allocative inefficiency — underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss.
  • Output lies left of minimum AC, so there is productive inefficiency.

But P > AC means supernormal profit that can be reinvested in R&D — the potential for dynamic efficiency.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with market power producing where MC equals MR, short of both the productively efficient point at minimum average cost and the allocatively efficient point where demand crosses marginal cost, with supernormal profit shaded

cards.front: Evaluate: is perfect competition more efficient than imperfect competition?
cards.back:
Statically, yes: long-run equilibrium is both allocatively and productively efficient, while a firm with market power is neither — and, shielded from competition, it may drift into X-inefficiency.

Dynamically, the ranking can reverse: only supernormal profit sustained into the long run funds R&D and innovation, and perfect competition competes that profit away. The trade-off is static efficiency today against dynamic efficiency tomorrow.

cards.front: Give the four characteristics of perfect competition — and what they make the firm.
cards.back:
Many buyers and sellers (each firm negligibly small), homogeneous products, perfect information, and freedom of entry and exit.

Together these make every firm a price taker: it accepts the market price as given and cannot influence it through its own actions.

cards.front: Show why a firm in perfect competition is a price taker.
cards.back:
The market panel sets the price: industry supply and demand cross at P1. The firm can sell any quantity at P1 and none above it, so its demand curve is perfectly elastic — horizontal at the market price.

That one line is the firm's D = AR = MR: every extra unit sells at exactly P1.
cards.svgAlt: Two panels: industry supply and demand set the market price, and the individual firm faces a horizontal demand curve at that price, so demand, average revenue and marginal revenue are the same line

cards.front: Show short-run supernormal profit in perfect competition.
cards.back:
The firm produces at Q1, where MC crosses the horizontal price line (its MR). Average cost C1 at that output lies below the price, so the shaded rectangle (P1 − C1) × Q1 is supernormal profit.

It cannot last: with no barriers, entry shifts industry supply right and the market price falls.
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition firm producing where marginal cost crosses the horizontal price line, with average cost below the price and the rectangle between them shaded as supernormal profit

cards.front: Show a short-run loss in perfect competition.
cards.back:
At Q1, where MC crosses the horizontal price line, average cost C1 sits above the price: the shaded rectangle (C1 − P1) × Q1 is the loss.

Losses drive firms out; industry supply shifts left and the market price rises until the firms that remain break even again.
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition firm where average cost lies above the horizontal price line at the output where marginal cost crosses it, with the rectangle between them shaded as the loss

cards.front: Trace the adjustment from short-run supernormal profit to long-run equilibrium in perfect competition.
cards.back:
Supernormal profit attracts new firms, which can enter freely. Industry supply shifts right, so the market price falls — and the firm's horizontal demand curve falls with it, until it is tangent to the minimum point of the AC curve. There P = AR = AC = MC and only normal profit remains.

From a short-run loss the chain runs in reverse: firms exit, supply shifts left and the price rises to the same long-run equilibrium.

cards.front: Show the long-run equilibrium of a firm in perfect competition.
cards.back:
Entry and exit stop when firms earn normal profit only: the horizontal price line is tangent to AC at its minimum, with MC through the same point, so P = AR = MR = AC = MC at Q.

The same diagram shows why this equilibrium is allocatively efficient (P = MC) and productively efficient (minimum AC).
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition long-run equilibrium with the horizontal price line tangent to the minimum of average cost where marginal cost also crosses, so price equals both marginal and average cost and only normal profit is earned

cards.front: Give the characteristics of monopolistic competition — and what they mean for the firm's demand curve.
cards.back:
Many firms each with a small market share, product differentiation (similar core products set apart by branding, quality, features or marketing) and low barriers to entry and exit. Think restaurants, clothing brands, hairdressers.

Differentiation gives each firm a little market power: it is a price maker facing a downward-sloping demand (AR) curve.

cards.front: Show the short-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition.
cards.back:
The firm maximises profit where MC = MR. In the short run it can earn supernormal profit — price read off AR above average cost read off AC, the shaded rectangle.

It can equally make a loss in the short run if AR sits below AC at that output. Neither outcome survives the long run, because entry and exit are almost free.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with output where MC equals MR and the price from AR above average cost from AC, shading supernormal profit — the short-run position available to a monopolistically competitive firm

cards.front: Show the long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition.
cards.back:
Supernormal profit attracts entrants, which take market share and shift each firm's demand curve left until only normal profit remains (losses run the same process in reverse). In long-run equilibrium AR = AC at the profit-maximising output — the AC curve is tangent to the demand curve above Q.

In the exam you may show this by shifting only the AC curve until it touches AR at that output, as here.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram where the average cost curve is tangent to the downward-sloping demand curve exactly above the output where MC equals MR, so the firm earns only normal profit

cards.front: Is monopolistic competition efficient?
cards.back:
In long-run equilibrium, no on all three counts: not productively efficient (output is not at minimum AC), not allocatively efficient (P > MC), and dynamic efficiency is limited because only normal profit is earned in the long run — though short-run supernormal profits may fund some R&D.

Competition itself is the consolation: many rivals and easy entry help keep prices down.

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of monopolistic competition on consumers.
cards.back:
• Prices can go either way: differentiation, branding and weak economies of scale push them up; many firms and easy entry push them down.
  • Quality likewise: competition forces firms to differentiate and improve, but normal-profit margins leave little to invest.
  • Choice is the clearest gain — many differentiated products — though differentiation can be surface-level, so the variety is not always meaningful.

cards.front: Give the key characteristics of oligopoly.
cards.back:
A few large firms dominate (a high concentration ratio), there are high barriers to entry, products are differentiated, and — the defining feature — firms are interdependent: each must weigh rivals' likely reactions before setting price, output or marketing.

Interdependence is why oligopoly needs its own tools: game theory, and the choice between colluding and competing. Think UK supermarkets, airlines, mobile networks.

cards.front: What is a concentration ratio, and how is it calculated?
cards.back:
A concentration ratio measures the degree of market concentration: the n-firm ratio is the share of total market sales held by the largest n firms. A 3-firm ratio of 80% means the top three firms account for 80% of the market's sales.

A higher ratio marks a more concentrated, generally less competitive market.
cards.formulaHtml: n−firmCR=(revenueoftopnfirms÷totalmarketrevenue)×100n-firm CR = (revenue of top n firms ÷ total market revenue) × 100n−firmCR=(revenueoftopnfirms÷totalmarketrevenue)×100

cards.front: A market's total sales are £800m. The four largest firms sell £260m, £180m, £120m and £90m; the remaining firms share the rest. Calculate the 4-firm concentration ratio.
cards.back:
Sales of the top four: 260 + 180 + 120 + 90 = £650m.

The 4-firm ratio = 650 ÷ 800 × 100 = 81.25%.

Four firms supply just over four-fifths of the market — a highly concentrated oligopoly whose members will be strongly interdependent.

cards.front: Distinguish overt and tacit collusion.
cards.back:
Collusion is firms agreeing — formally or informally — to restrict supply and raise price, acting like a monopoly to earn supernormal profit.

Overt collusion is a formal agreement (a cartel): illegal and provable in court, as when British Airways and Virgin Atlantic fixed fuel surcharges in 2007.

Tacit collusion is an informal understanding, often via price leadership — the market leader sets a price and rivals follow. Same outcome, far harder to prove.

cards.front: Show the effect of collusion on price, output and welfare.
cards.back:
Colluding firms act like a monopoly: output is restricted to Qcoll, where MC = MR, and price rises to Pcoll — against the competitive outcome at Qcomp, where MC crosses demand (P = MC), with the lower price Pcomp.

Units between Qcoll and Qcomp that society values above their cost are no longer made: the shaded triangle between D and MC is the deadweight welfare loss from collusion.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram comparing the collusive outcome, restricted output and higher price where MC equals MR, with the competitive outcome where MC crosses demand, and the deadweight loss triangle between them shaded

cards.front: Use the kinked demand curve to explain price rigidity in a competitive oligopoly.
cards.back:
• Above the current price demand is elastic: rivals ignore a price rise, so customers switch away and revenue falls.
  • Below it demand is inelastic: rivals match a cut, so few customers arrive and revenue still falls — at worst a price war starts.

The kink makes MR discontinuous at Q, and MC can shift anywhere within the gap without changing the profit-maximising price — so prices stay "sticky" and firms compete through differentiation and advertising instead.
cards.svgAlt: Demand curve kinked at the current price, elastic above and inelastic below, with a vertical gap in marginal revenue at the kink output through which the MC curve passes

cards.front: Name and define the types of price competition in oligopoly.
cards.back:
• Price wars — repeated rounds of undercutting that damage every firm's profits.
  • Predatory pricing — temporarily pricing below average cost to drive smaller rivals out and raise prices later; illegal in the UK and US.
  • Limit pricing — pricing low enough that large supernormal profits are unattainable, deterring entry.

Because price competition is so costly, oligopolists usually prefer non-price competition: differentiation, advertising, customer service, convenience and loyalty schemes.

cards.front: Use the prisoner's dilemma to explain why collusion in oligopoly is unstable.
cards.back:
If Samsung and Apple both hold high prices they earn £150bn each — the collusive outcome. But whichever firm undercuts earns £200bn while its rival slumps to £50bn, so cutting price is each firm's dominant strategy.

Both cut, and the market settles at the Nash equilibrium: £100bn each, worse than collusion for both. Sustaining a cartel therefore needs trust and communication — which is exactly what rivals lack.
cards.svgAlt: Two-by-two payoff matrix for Samsung and Apple choosing high or low prices: both high earns 150 billion pounds each, one undercutting earns 200 billion against 50 billion, and the Nash equilibrium at both low prices earns 100 billion each

cards.front: Define monopoly — pure and legal.
cards.back:
A pure monopoly is a market structure where there is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes — think a local water company. High barriers to entry protect its supernormal profit, and it is a price maker.

A legal (working) monopoly is defined by the CMA as a firm with 25% or more market share — Google's 90%-plus share of UK search comfortably qualifies.

cards.front: Show the profit-maximising equilibrium of a monopoly.
cards.back:
The monopolist produces where MC = MR and charges the price on the demand curve above it — P > MC, with supernormal profit shaded between price and average cost.

Unlike more competitive structures, barriers to entry let this profit persist into the long run: no entrants arrive to compete it away.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with output where MC equals MR and price read from the demand curve above average cost, shading the supernormal profit a monopoly can sustain in the long run

cards.front: Assess each type of efficiency under monopoly.
cards.back:
• Allocative: no — output is where MC = MR rather than AR = MC, so P > MC and there is a welfare loss to society.
  • Productive: no — output is not at the lowest point of AC.
  • X-inefficiency: possible — with little competition, costs may drift above their minimum.
  • Dynamic: yes — long-run supernormal profit gives both the means and the motive to invest in R&D, the monopolist's strongest defence.

cards.front: What is third-degree price discrimination, and what three conditions make it possible?
cards.back:
Charging different consumer groups different prices for the same product — by age, location or time of use — to increase total profit.

It needs: (1) market power, so few or no substitutes; (2) sub-markets with different PEDs the firm can identify — peak against off-peak travel, student against adult tickets; (3) the ability to separate the markets and prevent resale, often through ID.

cards.front: Show how third-degree price discrimination raises a monopolist's profit.
cards.back:
In each sub-market the firm sells where MR = MC and reads the price off that group's demand curve: the inelastic group (steep D — peak travellers) pays the high price; the elastic group (flatter D — off-peak) pays less.

The two shaded rectangles together exceed the single-price profit, because pricing by group captures more consumer surplus. Inelastic-demand customers pay more and lose surplus; elastic-demand customers pay less and gain; and the extra profit can fund R&D — the firm's standard defence.
cards.svgAlt: Two panels sharing one horizontal AC equals MC line: the steep inelastic sub-market pays a high price and the flatter elastic sub-market a lower one, with each group's profit rectangle shaded

cards.front: Evaluate: who gains and who loses from monopoly?
cards.back:
• The firm gains economies of scale and lasting supernormal profit for R&D — but invites regulation, X-inefficiency and public backlash.
  • Consumers typically face higher prices, lower output and less choice, yet can gain if scale economies cut costs or profits fund innovation.
  • Workers may enjoy more secure, better-paid jobs in a protected firm — or find the lack of competition limits wages and progression.
  • Suppliers get stable demand and long contracts, but face a buyer with the power to squeeze prices and delay payment.

cards.front: What is a natural monopoly? Show why competition is inefficient there.
cards.back:
An industry with such a high proportion of fixed costs — water, rail, energy grids — that LRAC falls over the entire range of market demand: one firm can always supply the market more cheaply than several could.

The diagram shows the regulator's dilemma:

  • A private profit-maximiser produces Qp at the high price Pp (grey guides).
  • Pricing at P = MC (red guides, output Qn) is allocatively efficient but sets price below average cost, a loss needing subsidy.

Theme 3.6.1 picks this up.
cards.svgAlt: Natural monopoly diagram with long-run average cost falling over the whole market and marginal cost below it: private profit maximisation gives low output and a high price, while pricing at marginal cost gives high output but a price below average cost

cards.front: Define monopsony — and give its key characteristics.
cards.back:
A monopsony is a market with a single buyer of a good, service, or factor of production — a big supermarket chain buying from farmers, or the NHS hiring nurses.

As the dominant buyer it is a wage or price maker: it chooses how much to hire or buy to maximise profit, typically paying lower wages or prices — and employing fewer workers — than a competitive market would.

cards.front: Evaluate the costs and benefits of monopsony power for each stakeholder.
cards.back:
• The firm gains lower input costs and higher profits — at the risk of demotivated workers and a damaged public image.
  • Consumers can see lower prices from those lower costs, but quality and choice may suffer if the buyer's grip tightens.
  • Workers face lower wages and weaker job security, unless regulation protects them.
  • Suppliers get stable demand and long-term contracts, but with weak bargaining power: squeezed prices and delayed payment.

cards.front: What is a contestable market — and how does contestability differ from competition?
cards.back:
A contestable market is one with freedom of entry and exit. What disciplines firms is the threat of potential competition, not the number of firms currently in the market.

The distinction:

  • Competition is about how many firms there are.
  • Contestability is about how easily firms can enter and leave.

A concentrated market can still behave competitively if it is highly contestable — Amazon and eBay both do.

cards.front: Give the characteristics of a contestable market.
cards.back:
No (or very low) barriers to entry and exit, minimal sunk costs, no competitive disadvantage for entrants — they can access the same technology and resources as incumbents — and perfect information.

Together these make hit-and-run competition possible: a firm enters quickly to take short-run supernormal profit and leaves once profits return to normal — and the mere possibility keeps incumbents behaving competitively.

cards.front: Show limit pricing — how an incumbent deters entry in a contestable market.
cards.back:
Rather than profit-maximising at MC = MR, the incumbent sets price down at the output where AR = AC, earning only normal profit — the same point a sales-maximiser chooses.

With no supernormal profit on display, there is no profit signal to attract entrants.

The more contestable the market, the closer behaviour drifts towards the perfectly competitive outcome: lower prices, higher output, greater allocative efficiency.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the chosen point at the output where average revenue equals average cost, so only normal profit is earned and no supernormal profit remains to attract new entrants

cards.front: What are sunk costs — and why do they decide how contestable a market is?
cards.back:
Sunk costs are costs that cannot be recovered if a firm leaves the market — specialised machinery, advertising, research and development.

They are the main barrier to exit: the higher they are, the riskier entry becomes, so the less contestable the market.

Other barriers work on the way in:

  • Economies of scale.
  • High start-up costs.
  • Legal barriers.
  • Brand loyalty.
  • Control of key resources.
  • Anti-competitive practices.

cards.front: Define the demand for labour — and why is it a derived demand?
cards.back:
Demand for labour: the quantity of workers that firms are willing and able to employ at a given wage rate.

It is a derived demand: firms want workers not for their own sake but for the goods and services labour produces — so demand for the final product drives demand for the labour that makes it.

cards.front: State the marginal revenue product formula — and define its parts.
cards.back:
MRP = MPP × MR

  • Marginal physical product (MPP) is the extra output produced by one more worker.
  • Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue gained from selling that extra output.

The MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour, D(L) — and it slopes downward because of the law of diminishing returns.
cards.formulaHtml: MRP=MPP×MRMRP = MPP × MRMRP=MPP×MR

cards.front: A firm sells output at a constant £4 per unit. Total output is 18 with one worker, 40 with two, 57 with three and 68 with four. Calculate each worker's MRP — and how many workers are hired at a wage of £50?
cards.back:
MPP: 18, 22, 17, 11. MRP = MPP × £4: £72, £88, £68, £44.

Hire while MRP is at least the wage: the third worker adds £68 (≥ £50) but the fourth only £44 (< £50), so the firm employs three workers. Diminishing returns after the second worker is what bends the MRP — and so the labour demand curve — downward.

cards.front: Show the demand curve for labour.
cards.back:
The curve D(L) = MRP plots the marginal revenue product of each extra worker against the wage. It slopes downward because of diminishing returns: each extra worker adds less output, so less revenue.

A wage change moves the firm along the curve — at W1 it hires Q1, at the lower W2 it hires Q2 — while anything changing MRP itself shifts the whole curve.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping labour demand curve labelled D of L equals MRP, with a high wage W1 giving employment Q1 and a lower wage W2 giving the larger employment Q2

cards.front: What shifts the demand curve for labour?
cards.back:
Anything that changes labour's MRP: higher demand for the final product (the derived-demand link) or a higher product price raises MRP and shifts D(L) right; higher labour productivity does the same through MPP.

Better substitutes work the other way: if capital becomes a stronger substitute for labour, the demand for labour shifts left.

cards.front: What makes the demand for labour wage-elastic?
cards.back:
Labour demand responds more to wage changes when:

  • The final product's demand is price elastic, so wage-driven price rises lose many sales.
  • Capital can easily substitute for labour.
  • Labour is a large share of total costs, so a wage change moves total costs significantly.

It is also more elastic over a longer time period, when firms have time to reorganise production.

cards.front: Define the supply of labour — and how do market and individual supply curves differ?
cards.back:
Supply of labour: the quantity of workers willing and able to work at a given wage rate.

For a market or occupation the curve slopes upward — higher wages draw more workers in. For an individual it can bend backwards at very high wages, where the income effect overtakes the substitution effect.

cards.front: Show the market and individual labour supply curves — and explain the backward bend.
cards.back:
The substitution effect of a wage rise: leisure becomes more expensive, so work more hours. The income effect: the same living standard now takes fewer hours, so work less.

At low wages substitution dominates and the curve rises; at very high wages the income effect wins and the individual's curve bends backwards — hours fall back from Q2 as the wage climbs past W2. The market curve stays upward sloping throughout.
cards.svgAlt: Two panels: an upward-sloping market labour supply curve, and an individual supply curve that rises to a maximum quantity at wage W2 and then bends backwards at higher wages

cards.front: What shifts the supply curve of labour to an occupation?
cards.back:
Anything other than the wage that changes willingness or ability to do the job:

  • Monetary benefits (bonuses, overtime, stock options).
  • Non-monetary benefits (conditions, flexible hours, healthcare).
  • Demographic change and migration policy (the size of the available workforce).
  • Education and training (who is qualified).
  • Taxation and welfare (the incentive to work at all).

cards.front: How does labour immobility cause market failure?
cards.back:
• Geographical immobility — workers cannot move to where the jobs are (house prices and rent, transport costs, information gaps).
  • Occupational immobility — skills do not transfer between industries (training and qualification requirements, technological change).

Both leave vacancies unfilled beside workers unemployed: structural unemployment and skill shortages.

Policy answers: education, apprenticeships and careers guidance for occupational mobility; subsidised housing, relocation help and better transport for geographical.

cards.front: What determines the wage elasticity of labour supply?
cards.back:
Supply responds more to wage changes when the time period is longer (time to retrain or relocate), when workers are occupationally and geographically mobile, and when there is a large pool of suitable unemployed labour to draw on.

It is less elastic for vocational occupations needing specific skills or qualifications — a pay rise cannot recruit surgeons this year.

cards.front: Show wage determination in a competitive labour market.
cards.back:
Many firms demand labour and many workers supply it, so both sides are wage takers: the equilibrium wage W1 and employment Q1 sit where D(L) = MRP crosses S(L) = AC.

Everything else in this unit — monopsony, trade unions, the minimum wage — is a departure from this benchmark.
cards.svgAlt: Labour market diagram with the upward-sloping supply curve and downward-sloping demand curve crossing at the equilibrium wage W1 and employment Q1

cards.front: Show how a monopsony sets wages and employment.
cards.back:
Facing the whole supply curve, the monopsonist must raise everyone's pay to hire one more worker, so MCL lies above S = AC. It hires Qm, where MCL = MRP, but pays only Wm — the wage on the supply curve at Qm. Both wage and employment sit below the competitive Wc and Qc.

The gap between MRP at Qm (the height W1) and Wm is monopsonistic exploitation: each worker is paid less than the value of what they produce.
cards.svgAlt: Monopsony labour market diagram with the marginal cost of labour rising above the supply curve, employment where MCL crosses MRP, and the wage read off the supply curve below the competitive wage

cards.front: What is a trade union, and how is union density calculated?
cards.back:
A trade union is an organisation formed by workers to protect their rights, improve pay and secure better working conditions — using collective bargaining backed by the threat of industrial action.

Union density — members as a share of the total workforce — measures its power, alongside the union's size, the firm's profitability, the state of the economy and the stance of government policy.
cards.formulaHtml: Uniondensity=(unionmembers÷totalworkforce)×100Union density = (union members ÷ total workforce) × 100Uniondensity=(unionmembers÷totalworkforce)×100

cards.front: Show a trade union in a competitive labour market.
cards.back:
The union negotiates W(TU) above the equilibrium W1. Employers hire only Qd at that wage, while Qs workers want jobs: employment falls from Q1, and the surplus Qs − Qd is real wage unemployment.

Members who keep their jobs win higher pay; the cost lands on those priced out of work.
cards.svgAlt: Labour market diagram with a trade union wage set above equilibrium, cutting employment to Qd while Qs workers seek jobs, the gap being real wage unemployment

cards.front: Show a trade union facing a monopsony employer.
cards.back:
Union and monopsonist form a bilateral monopoly — a single seller of labour against a single buyer. The negotiated wage W(TU) makes the effective labour cost flat out to Qc (hiring another worker no longer raises everyone's pay), where it rejoins the supply curve and jumps up to the old MCL.

With MCL flattened, the profit-maximising hire rises from Qm to Qc while the wage rises from Wm to W(TU) — countering monopsony power, a union can raise both wages and employment.
cards.svgAlt: Monopsony labour market with a union wage drawn as a flat red line out to Qc, then a vertical jump up to the original marginal cost of labour, raising both the wage and employment compared with the monopsony outcome

cards.front: Show the impact of a national minimum wage on the labour market.
cards.back:
The NMW is a legally enforced price floor at Wmin, above the equilibrium W1. Workers who keep their jobs earn more, reducing income inequality — but labour demanded contracts to QD while supply extends to QS, so QS − QD is real wage unemployment.

Employment falls from Q1 to QD: the gains go to those still employed, the cost to those the higher wage prices out.
cards.svgAlt: Labour market diagram with a national minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage, cutting labour demanded to QD while labour supplied extends to QS, the gap being real wage unemployment

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of a national minimum wage.
cards.back:
• It depends on the size of the rise: far above equilibrium means big income gains but substantial real wage unemployment.
  • It depends on the wage elasticity of labour demand: with inelastic demand few jobs are lost, so the policy works best where demand is wage inelastic.
  • And it depends on motivation: if higher pay lifts productivity, the rise in firms' average costs — and the job losses — shrink.

The elasticities of labour demand and supply decide how any labour market intervention plays out.

cards.front: What is the CMA, and how does it control mergers?
cards.back:
The Competition and Markets Authority is the main independent regulator of markets in the UK: it investigates anti-competitive practices, reviews mergers and enforces consumer protection law.

It can block a merger that would create a firm with 25% or more market share or substantially lessen competition — or force the merged firm to sell assets. It blocked Sainsbury's–Asda in 2019 over fears grocery and fuel prices would rise.

cards.front: How do price regulation and profit regulation control a monopoly?
cards.back:
Price regulation: a price cap such as RPI−X lets the monopoly raise prices only by inflation minus an efficiency factor X — forcing it below the profit-maximising price. Risk: less to invest, or costs cut so hard that quality falls.

Profit regulation, often a cap set as a share of revenue, pushes prices towards average cost. Risk: rather than cut prices, the firm lets costs inflate to shrink its measured margin — and consumers see no gain.

cards.front: How do quality standards and performance targets regulate a monopoly?
cards.back:
The regulator sets minimum service or quality standards — say, a percentage of trains arriving on time — with large fines for missing the targets. This tackles the monopolist's temptation to let quality slide when customers have nowhere else to go.

Watch for unintended consequences: firms may hit the target by offering high quality only at high prices, pricing out lower-income households.

cards.front: How can government promote competition and contestability?
cards.back: Promoting small businesses (grants, tax breaks, advice), deregulation (removing entry barriers — as when Royal Mail lost its legal protection over parcels), competitive tendering (putting government contracts out to open bidding), and privatisation (selling state-owned assets so profit incentives and competition drive efficiency).

cards.front: Show nationalisation against privatisation of a natural monopoly.
cards.back:
With LRAC falling over the whole market, a privatised profit-maximiser produces Qp, where MR = LRMC, at the high price Pp (grey guides). A nationalised firm pricing at P = MC produces the much larger Qn at the lower price Pn (red guides) — allocatively efficient, but Pn sits below average cost Cn, so the state subsidises the loss.

Privatisation swaps that subsidy for profit incentives and potential efficiency — at the risk of higher prices and lower output.
cards.svgAlt: Natural monopoly diagram comparing a private profit maximiser's low output and high price with a nationalised firm pricing at marginal cost, whose larger output comes at a price below average cost

cards.front: Evaluate: does privatisation benefit consumers?
cards.back:
• For: shareholder pressure creates a profit incentive that can drive productive efficiency, lower prices, and — through reinvested profit — dynamic efficiency and better quality.
  • Against: the firm no longer exists to serve everyone; with weak competition it may raise prices and cut quality.

The verdict turns on competition and contestability (parcel delivery, yes; water, no) and on the effectiveness of regulation — which itself depends on avoiding regulatory capture.

cards.front: How can government protect suppliers and employees from market power?
cards.back:
Suppliers facing a monopsony buyer:

  • Minimum prices (a legal price floor).
  • Support for cooperatives so suppliers can bargain together.
  • Merger control to stop monopsony power growing.

Employees:

  • The national minimum wage.
  • Employment legislation (health and safety, working hours, unfair dismissal).
  • Support for trade unions.
  • Pay transparency requirements that pressure employers towards fair wages.

cards.front: What impacts is government intervention in markets trying to achieve?
cards.back:
• Prices: lower, so essentials stay affordable at every income.
  • Quality: higher, through investment and innovation.
  • Choice: wider, improving allocative efficiency.
  • Profit: controlled — enough to fund reinvestment, not extracted at consumers' expense.
  • Efficiency: better productive and allocative efficiency.

Every intervention in 3.6.1 is judged against these five yardsticks.

cards.front: What is regulatory capture, and what causes it?
cards.back:
Regulatory capture: regulated firms gain so much influence over their regulator that the rules end up shaped in the firms' favour rather than consumers'.

Two causes:

  • Asymmetric information — the regulator depends on the firm's own data, which the firm can present selectively.
  • The "revolving door", where regulators soften rules hoping for future jobs in the industry.

The result is regulation that is too lenient to bite.

cards.front: Evaluate the limits of government intervention in markets.
cards.back:
• Asymmetric information: regulators know less than the firms they police, so policies end up poorly targeted, easy to dodge or costly.
  • Administrative costs can exceed the benefits.
  • Unintended consequences: caps and rules can choke innovation, quality or competition.
  • Conflicting objectives: a price cap that helps consumers today can starve investment tomorrow.

When intervention makes the outcome worse than the market failure it targeted, that is government failure.
